Appendix D Further Analysis of the Embedding Loss

In this section, we provide a complete mathematical derivation of the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) loss used in our embedding framework, progressing from theoretical foundations to practical implementation.

D.1 Theoretical Foundation of MMD in RKHS

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} denote a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) with kernel function k:𝒳×𝒳→ℝk:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and feature map φ:𝒳→ℋ\varphi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}. The kernel satisfies the reproducing property:

k⁡(x,y)=⟨φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)⟩ℋk(x,y)=\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} (52)

The Maximum Mean Discrepancy between two distributions PP and QQ measures the distance between their mean embeddings in ℋ\mathcal{H}:

DMMD​[P,Q]=‖𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)]−𝔼y∼Q​[φ⁡(y)]‖ℋD_{\text{MMD}}[P,Q]=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[\varphi(y)]\right\|_{\mathcal{H}} (53)

D.2 Derivation of Squared MMD

Squaring the MMD and expanding the norm:

DMMD2​[P,Q]\displaystyle D_{\textit{MMD}}^{2}[P,Q] =‖𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)]−𝔼y∼Q​[φ⁡(y)]‖ℋ2\displaystyle=\left\|\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[\varphi(y)]\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} (54)
=⟨𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)]−𝔼y∼Q​[φ⁡(y)],𝔼x′∼P​[φ⁡(x′)]−𝔼y′∼Q​[φ⁡(y′)]⟩ℋ\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[\varphi(y)],\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim P}[\varphi(x^{\prime})]-\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim Q}[\varphi(y^{\prime})]\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}

Expanding the inner product into four terms:

DMMD2​(P,Q)\displaystyle D_{\text{MMD}}^{2}(P,Q) =⟨𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)],𝔼x′∼P​[φ⁡(x′)]⟩ℋ−2​⟨𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)],𝔼y∼Q​[φ⁡(y)]⟩ℋ+⟨𝔼y∼Q​[φ⁡(y)],𝔼y′∼Q​[φ⁡(y′)]⟩ℋ\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)],\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim P}[\varphi(x^{\prime})]\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-2\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)],\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[\varphi(y)]\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim Q}[\varphi(y)],\mathbb{E}_{y^{\prime}\sim Q}[\varphi(y^{\prime})]\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} (55)

By applying the reproducing property and exchanging expectation with inner product:

⟨𝔼x∼P​[φ⁡(x)],𝔼x′∼P​[φ⁡(x′)]⟩ℋ=𝔼x,x′∼P​[⟨φ⁡(x),φ⁡(x′)⟩ℋ]=𝔼x,x′∼P​[k⁡(x,x′)]\left\langle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P}[\varphi(x)],\mathbb{E}_{x^{\prime}\sim P}[\varphi(x^{\prime})]\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim P}\left[\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(x^{\prime})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim P}[k(x,x^{\prime})] (56)

This yields the expectation form:

DMMD2​(P,Q)=𝔼x,x′∼P​[k⁡(x,x′)]−2​𝔼x∼Py∼Q​[k⁡(x,y)]+𝔼y,y′∼Q​[k⁡(y,y′)]D_{\textit{MMD}}^{2}(P,Q)=\mathbb{E}_{x,x^{\prime}\sim P}[k(x,x^{\prime})]-2\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim P\\ y\sim Q\end{subarray}}[k(x,y)]+\mathbb{E}_{y,y^{\prime}\sim Q}[k(y,y^{\prime})] (57)

D.3 Multi-scale Kernel Formulation

To enhance robustness across different scales, we introduce a mixture over the bandwidth parameter σ\sigma, sampled from a uniform distribution UU with density r⁡(σ)r(\sigma):

DMMD2​(P,Q)\displaystyle D_{\textit{MMD}}^{2}(P,Q) =𝔼x,x′∼Pσ∼U[k(x,x′;σ)]−2𝔼x∼P,y∼Qσ∼U[k(x,y;σ)]+𝔼y,y′∼Qσ∼U[k(y,y′;σ)]\displaystyle=\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x,x^{\prime}\sim P\\ \sigma\sim U\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[k(x,x^{\prime};\sigma)\right]-2\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim P,y\sim Q\\ \sigma\sim U\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[k(x,y;\sigma)\right]\quad+\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}y,y^{\prime}\sim Q\\ \sigma\sim U\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}\left[k(y,y^{\prime};\sigma)\right] (58)

In integral form with probability densities p⁡(x)p(x) and q⁡(y)q(y):

DMMD2​(P,Q)=\displaystyle D_{\textit{MMD}}^{2}(P,Q)= ∭p⁡(x)​p​(x′)​r​(σ)​k​(x,x′,σ)​𝑑x​d​x′​𝑑σ\displaystyle\iiint p(x)p(x^{\prime})r(\sigma)k(x,x^{\prime};\sigma)\,dx\,dx^{\prime}\,d\sigma (59)
−2\displaystyle-2 ∭p⁡(x)​q​(y)​r​(σ)​k​(x,y,σ)​𝑑x​𝑑y​𝑑σ\displaystyle\iiint p(x)q(y)r(\sigma)k(x,y;\sigma)\,dx\,dy\,d\sigma
+\displaystyle+ ∭q⁡(y)​q​(y′)​r​(σ)​k​(y,y′,σ)​𝑑y​d​y′​𝑑σ\displaystyle\iiint q(y)q(y^{\prime})r(\sigma)k(y,y^{\prime};\sigma)\,dy\,dy^{\prime}\,d\sigma

D.4 Empirical Estimation

In practice, given an embedding function ψ(i)\psi^{(i)} and parameter σ\sigma, we work with finite samples from the embedded space samples P(i),Q(i)P^{(i)},Q^{(i)}: {x1,…,xm}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\} from P(i)P^{(i)}, {y1,…,yn}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}\} from Q(i)Q^{(i)}, and {σ1,…,σr}\{\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}\} bandwidth values. The empirical estimator is:

D^MMD2​(P(i),Q(i))\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\textit{MMD}^{2}}(P^{(i)},Q^{(i)}) =1r​∑i=1r(1N12​∑k=1N1∑l=1N1k⁡(xk,xl,σi)−2​1N1​N2​∑k=1N1∑l=1N2k⁡(xk,yl,σi)+1N22​∑k=1N2∑l=1N2k⁡(yk,yl,σi))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Bigg(\frac{1}{N_{1}^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{1}}\sum_{l=1}^{N_{1}}k(x_{k},x_{l};\sigma_{i})-2\frac{1}{N_{1}N_{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{1}}\sum_{l=1}^{N_{2}}k(x_{k},y_{l};\sigma_{i})+\frac{1}{N_{2}^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{N_{2}}\sum_{l=1}^{N_{2}}k(y_{k},y_{l};\sigma_{i})\Bigg) (60)

D.5 Pairwise Distance Formulation

For a single pair of samples (x,y)(x,y), the squared MMD distance in feature space is:

D^MMD2​(x,y,σ)\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\textit{MMD}^{2}}(x,y;\sigma) =‖φ⁡(x)−φ⁡(y)‖ℋ2\displaystyle=\|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} (61)
=⟨φ⁡(x),φ⁡(x)⟩ℋ−2​⟨φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)⟩ℋ+⟨φ⁡(y),φ⁡(y)⟩ℋ\displaystyle=\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-2\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\varphi(y),\varphi(y)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
=k⁡(x,x,σ)−2​k​(x,y,σ)+k⁡(y,y,σ)\displaystyle=k(x,x;\sigma)-2k(x,y;\sigma)+k(y,y;\sigma)

D.6 RBF Kernel Implementation

We employ the Radial Basis Function (Gaussian) kernel:

k⁡(x,y,σ)=exp⁡(−‖x−y‖222​σ2)k(x,y;\sigma)=\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) (62)

where the inner product in feature space becomes:

⟨φ⁡(x),φ⁡(y)⟩ℋ=k⁡(x,y,σ)=exp⁡(−‖x−y‖222​σ2)\langle\varphi(x),\varphi(y)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=k(x,y;\sigma)=\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right) (63)

and the squared Euclidean distance is computed as:

‖x−y‖22=‖x‖22−2​x⊤​y+‖y‖22=x⊤​x−2​x⊤​y+y⊤​y\|x-y\|_{2}^{2}=\|x\|_{2}^{2}-2x^{\top}y+\|y\|_{2}^{2}=x^{\top}x-2x^{\top}y+y^{\top}y (64)

This formulation enables efficient computation of the embedding loss while maintaining theoretical guarantees provided by the RKHS framework. The multi-scale kernel approach ensures robustness to variations in data scale, making the loss particularly suitable for our embedding learning task.

D.6.1 Practical Implications

Corollary 4 (Why EL Improves Distillation): The embedding loss addresses the score gap Δ\Delta through three mechanisms:

  1. 1.

    Distribution Alignment: By minimizing MMD in multiple feature spaces, EL ensures pθ≈pdatap_{\theta}\approx p_{\text{data}} globally, which by Theorem 1 reduces ‖Δ‖\|\Delta\|.

  2. 2.

    Implicit Score Correction: By Theorem 3, the EL gradient provides sample-wise corrections in the direction of Δeff\Delta_{\text{eff}}, compensating for teacher model limitations.

  3. 3.

    Multi-scale Matching: Using diverse embeddings ℰ\mathcal{E}, EL captures distributional discrepancies at multiple scales and semantic levels, providing comprehensive coverage of the gap.

Proposition 1 (Advantage over Alternatives):

  • •

    vs. Regression Loss: Pure regression ℒreg=𝔼⁡[‖Gθ−fϕ‖2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}=\mathbb{E}[\|G_{\theta}-f_{\phi}\|^{2}] only ensures Gθ≈fϕG_{\theta}\approx f_{\phi} pointwise, inheriting all teacher limitations (including Δ\Delta). EL allows the student to exceed the teacher by directly matching pdatap_{\text{data}}.

  • •

    vs. GAN Loss: Adversarial training implicitly addresses Δ\Delta through a learned discriminator, but suffers from instability. EL provides stable, fixed-embedding-based distribution matching with similar theoretical guarantees.
